Note: In the developed Greek and Roman tradition, Attis is Cybele’s youthful consort and the mythic model for her eunuch devotees. Accounts vary in their genealogy and do not consistently make him her son. His madness, castration, and death or preservation became central to later ritual mourning and regeneration symbolism.

The Song of Kumarbi makes Teshub one of the gods generated after Kumarbi attacks Anu and receives Anu’s seed within his body. Kumarbi is therefore Teshub’s paradoxical father or gestational parent as well as the displaced ruler who repeatedly attempts to overthrow him.

The Hattian-Hittite Storm God and Illuyanka are the central divine adversaries of the serpent myth. The Storm God is first defeated and later overcomes Illuyanka through Inara and Hupasiya in one version and through the recovery of his heart and eyes in the other.

Aeneas is the son of Aphrodite and Anchises. In the Iliad and later tradition, Aphrodite repeatedly protects him, while his divine maternity helps explain his survival of Troy and his later role as a carrier of Trojan lineage.

In the broader Judgment of Paris tradition, Aphrodite promises Helen to Paris in return for his verdict and later supports their union. The connection makes divine desire an immediate mythic cause of the conflict that brings Helen to Troy.

Hector is the eldest and foremost warrior among Priam’s sons. Their relationship culminates after Hector’s death, when the aged Priam enters Achilles’ camp to ransom his son’s body and secure the funeral rites owed to Troy’s defender.

Through her marriage to Paris, Helen becomes Priam’s daughter-in-law. In the Iliad, Priam addresses her with unusual kindness and does not personally blame her for the war, creating a compassionate relationship within the doomed Trojan household.

Greek legendary genealogy commonly presents Midas as the son or successor of Gordias, linking the humble, oracle-chosen founder with Phrygia’s fabulously wealthy king. The relationship belongs to dynastic legend and should not be treated as a securely documented historical genealogy.

Croesus succeeded his father Alyattes as king of Lydia around 560 BCE. Their successive reigns mark the height of Mermnad power, from Alyattes’s consolidation of the kingdom to Croesus’s expansion and eventual defeat by Persia.

Kumarbi is the central transitional ruler of the poem. He overthrows Anu, receives the seeds of a new divine generation through his violent attack, and becomes both the progenitor and future opponent of Teshub.

Kumarbi initiates the plot by generating Ullikummi as a new challenger to Teshub. The text presents him as a calculating displaced sovereign who uses a primordial stone being in another attempt to overturn the established divine order.
The Anitta Text explicitly invokes the Storm God of Heaven. Pithana is described as dear to the Storm God, and Anitta’s curse calls upon the deity to strike any future ruler who resettles Hattusa.

The Purulli festival tradition includes the Storm God’s struggle with Illuyanka as part of its ritual program. His defeat and recovery connect royal and priestly performance with the renewal, protection, and prosperity of the land.

The poem presents Teshub as a member of the new divine generation produced through Kumarbi’s attack on Anu. Although the text is fragmentary, Teshub emerges as the coming rival to Kumarbi’s claim to heavenly kingship.

The treaty invokes the Hittite Storm God or God of the Tempest as a divine sponsor of the peace established between Egypt and Hatti. The storm-god complex also belongs among the divine powers whose authority sacralizes and enforces the agreement.

The Storm God is the myth’s central divine protagonist. He is defeated by Illuyanka, regains the ability to fight through different forms of assistance in the two versions, and ultimately destroys the serpent at significant human cost.

Teshub appears as the established king challenged by Ullikummi. His storm weapons initially fail against the stone giant, and the gods must turn to Ea and the primordial cutting tool before resistance can continue.

The Purulli festival text preserves the recital of the Storm God’s confrontation with Illuyanka. The serpent’s defeat is incorporated into a spring ritual setting concerned with divine protection and the renewed well-being of the land.

Illuyanka is the serpent adversary named in both surviving versions. He defeats the Storm God at the beginning but is eventually killed—after being trapped at a feast in one account and after surrendering the god’s stolen heart and eyes in the other.

Both texts use the antiyant institution, in which a son-in-law can enter a household as heir. The laws attest the arrangement in family property practice, while the Edict of Telipinu adapts a comparable mechanism to royal succession when no male prince is available.

Both works belong to the scholarly grouping known as the Kumarbi Cycle. The Song of Kumarbi establishes the conflict between Kumarbi and the new generation led by Teshub, while the Song of Ullikummi presents a later attempt by Kumarbi to defeat that order.

The Illuyanka narrative is transmitted as the mythic component of a Purulli festival text. These entries therefore represent a contained narrative and its wider ritual framework rather than two unrelated traditions.

The Apology defends Hattusili III’s contested seizure of the Hittite throne, while the treaty recognizes him as Egypt’s equal royal partner and includes support for the succession of his son. Together they show domestic and international strategies for stabilizing his dynasty.
